For the life of St Paul, the {{c1::Pauline Epistles}} are the Primary Sources (direct, autobiographical, occasional).
For the life of St Paul, the {{c1::Acts of the Apostles}} by Luke is a Secondary Source (narrative, theological, retroactive).
The Delphi stone inscription of Emperor Claudius was discovered at the Temple of Apollo in {{c1::Delphi}} (Phocis), not in Corinth.
Paul stood before the judgment seat (bēma) of Proconsul Gallio in the city of {{c1::Corinth}} (Acts 18:12).
Lucius Junius Gallio Annaeus served as Roman Proconsul of the senatorial province of {{c1::Achaia}} between {{c2::Summer AD 51}} and {{c3::Summer AD 52}}.
The Gallio Inscription establishes that Emperor Claudius received his 26th imperial acclamation between {{c1::January}} and {{c2::August AD 52}}.
Because Paul ministered in Corinth for 18 months before his trial before Gallio (Acts 18:11), his arrival in Corinth is dated to {{c1::Autumn AD 50}}.
Paul's escape in a basket from Damascus (2 Cor 11:32 - 33) took place under the governor of the Nabataean King {{c1::Aretas IV}} between {{c2::AD 37 and 39}}.
The Judean famine predicted by Agabus (Acts 11:28), prompting Paul and Barnabas's relief visit to Jerusalem, occurred under Emperor Claudius in approximately {{c1::AD 44}}.
The imperial edict of Emperor Claudius expelling Jews from Rome (*Chrestus* agitation; Acts 18:2) was promulgated in {{c1::AD 49}}.
Paul's trial before Proconsul Gallio at Corinth (Acts 18:12) occurred during Gallio's annual tenure in {{c1::AD 51 - 52}}.
Paul's hearing in Caesarea before Procurator Porcius Festus, who succeeded Felix (Acts 24:27), took place in approximately {{c1::AD 58 - 60}}.
During his First Missionary Journey through Cyprus and southern Galatia (AD 46 - 48), Paul wrote {{c1::0}} surviving canonical letters.
From Corinth during his Second Missionary Journey (AD 49 - 52), Paul wrote the {{c1::Thessalonian Correspondence (1 & 2 Thess)}}.
From Ephesus, Macedonia, and Corinth during his Third Missionary Journey (AD 53 - 58), Paul wrote the four {{c1::Hauptbriefe (1 - 2 Cor, Gal, Rom)}}.
The optical external drama of Paul's Damascus encounter (blinding light, falling down, audible voice) is narrated only by {{c1::Luke in Acts (chs. 9, 22, 26)}}.
In his own letters (e.g. Gal 1:15 - 16; 1 Cor 9:1), Paul describes his Damascus encounter as an interior, prophetic {{c1::revelation (*apokalypsis*)}} of God's Son in him.
Paul's background in the city of {{c1::Tarsus}} gave him Hellenistic Koine Greek, Septuagintal literacy, Stoic rhetoric, and his manual tentmaking trade.
Paul's formation in {{c1::Jerusalem}} under Gamaliel gave him strict Pharisaic observance, rabbinic exegesis, and zeal for the ancestral traditions.
Paul's civic status as a {{c1::Roman citizen}} (by birth) provided legal protections against unexamined flogging and the right of appeal to Caesar.

In standard ancient epistolography, the opening prescript (*Praescriptum*) consists of three sub-elements: the Superscriptio (sender), the Adscriptio (recipient), and the {{c1::Salutatio (greeting)}}.
Paul transforms the conventional Greek secular greeting chairein into the Christian theological greeting {{c1::charis (grace)}}.
Paul complements the Greek greeting charis with the Hebrew greeting of covenant peace, {{c1::shalom (rendered eirēnē)}}.
Following the prescript, a canonical Pauline letter normally features an extended thanksgiving and prayer report known as the {{c1::Prooemium (or Eucharistia)}}.
The only canonical Pauline letter that completely omits the Prooemium due to apostolic indignation is {{c1::Galatians}} (replacing it with Thaumazō, "I am astonished!").
The doctrinal, kerygmatic, and theological argument of a Pauline letter is technically called the {{c1::Corpus Doctrinale}}.
The practical moral and pastoral exhortation of a Pauline letter, introduced by Parakalō ("I appeal"), is called the {{c1::Corpus Paraeneticum}}.
The concluding epistolary section containing greetings, holy kiss, autograph signature, and blessing is called the {{c1::Postscriptum (or Eschatokollon)}}.
The four traditional literary groupings of the 13 Pauline letters are: Eschatological, {{c1::Great Letters (Hauptbriefe)}}, Captivity, and Pastoral Epistles.
The two earliest epistles, comprising the Eschatological group, are {{c1::1 and 2 Thessalonians}}.
The four epistles comprising the Great Letters (Hauptbriefe) are 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, {{c1::Galatians}}, and {{c1::Romans}}.
Among the four Captivity Epistles, the two undisputed Proto-Pauline letters are {{c1::Philippians}} and {{c1::Philemon}}.
Among the four Captivity Epistles, the two letters widely categorized by modern historical criticism as Deutero-Pauline are {{c1::Colossians}} and {{c1::Ephesians}}.
The three Pastoral Epistles addressed to apostolic co-workers in Ephesus and Crete are {{c1::1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, and Titus}}.
The six letters classified as Deutero-Pauline by modern critical scholarship are 2 Thessalonians, Colossians, Ephesians, and the {{c1::three Pastoral Epistles (1 - 2 Tim, Titus)}}.
The only Christian scribe (amanuensis) who explicitly records his own personal greeting in Paul's letters is {{c1::Tertius}} (Romans 16:22).
Paul explicitly appends his autograph signature in 2 Thessalonians 3:17 as a verifiable {{c1::token (*sēmeion*)}} against fraudulent or forged letters.
The oldest surviving physical manuscript containing the collected Pauline epistles is {{c1::Papyrus 46 (𝔓⁴⁶ / Chester Beatty II)}}, dated c. AD 200.
Paul wrote 1 Thessalonians from the city of {{c1::Corinth}} around {{c2::AD 50 - 51}}, making it the chronologically earliest book of the New Testament.

In 1 Thessalonians 1:3, Paul pairs the three theological virtues with demanding actions: work of faith (*ergon pisteōs*), labour of love ({{c1::*kopos agapēs*}}), and steadfastness of hope (*hypomonē elpidos*).
In 1 Thessalonians 1:9 - 10, the pre-Pauline missionary kerygma defines conversion as turning from {{c1::idols}} to serve the living God, and waiting for His {{c2::Son}} from heaven.
In 1 Thessalonians 4:13, Paul softens the reality of death for believers by describing the deceased as those who have {{c1::fallen asleep (*koimōmenoi*)}}, establishing Christian hope.

In 1 Thessalonians 4:14, the bedrock foundation of Christian resurrection hope is formulated: *"For since we believe that {{c1::Jesus died and rose again}}, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with Him those who have fallen asleep."*
In 1 Thessalonians 4:17, Paul describes the meeting with the returning Lord using the Hellenistic civic welcoming term {{c1::*apantēsis* (ἀπάντησις)}}.
In 1 Thessalonians 5:2, Paul states that the Day of the Lord (*hēmera Kyriou*) will arrive unexpectedly, like a {{c1::thief in the night}}.
In 1 Thessalonians 5:3, Paul counters the Roman imperial slogan of {{c1::"Peace and Security" (*Pax et Securitas*)}} by warning of sudden apocalyptic labor pains.
In 1 Thessalonians 5:23, Paul prays for the complete sanctification of the believer across three dimensions: {{c1::spirit, soul, and body (*pneuma, psychē, sōma*)}}.
The pastoral crisis provoking 2 Thessalonians was panic caused by false claims that the {{c1::Day of the Lord had already come}} (2 Thess 2:2).
In 2 Thessalonians 2:6, the mysterious restraining power is designated with the neuter gender as {{c1::*to katechon* (τὸ κατέχον)}}.
In 2 Thessalonians 2:7, the mysterious restraining person is designated with the masculine gender as {{c1::*ho katechōn* (ὁ κατέχων)}}.
In 2 Thessalonians 3:10, Paul commands the disorderly community members: *"If anyone will not {{c1::work}}, neither shall he {{c2::eat}}."*
Strictly speaking, 1 Corinthians 13 is not a musical hymn, but belongs to the classical and biblical genre of the {{c1::aretologia}} (aretology, or praise of a virtue).
1 Corinthians 13 is framed by the dynamic verb of spiritual yearning, {{c1::zēloō}} (to desire/aspire), appearing in both 1 Cor 12:31 and 14:1.
In biblical Hebrew anthropology, the intellectual dimension of love from the head/vision is expressed by the verb {{c1::yāda‘}} (to know, cf. Psalm 139).
In biblical Hebrew anthropology, steadfast covenant tenderness and fidelity located in the heart (lēb) is expressed by {{c1::ḥesed}} (covenant love, cf. Ex 34:6).
In biblical Hebrew anthropology, visceral, maternal compassion derived from the womb (reḥem) is called {{c1::raḥamim}}.
In biblical Hebrew anthropology, love manifested in concrete diaconal labour and humble service is designated by {{c1::‘ebed}} (servant, cf. ‘Ebed Adonai in Isaiah 52–53).
In biblical theology, the four dimensions of love (head, heart, viscera, hands) unite in Hebrew ‘ahabah, which Saint Paul translates into Greek as {{c1::agapē}}.
In Humanae Vitae (no. 9), Saint Paul VI synthesised Christian marital love with four essential characteristics: love must be human, total, {{c1::faithful::[f...]}}, and fruitful.

In 1 Corinthians 13:1–3, Paul uses the {{c1::comparative::[comparative or descriptive?]}} method, demonstrating that without charity, even the highest charisms render a person {{c2::ouden eimi::[Greek: 'nothing']}}.

In 1 Corinthians 13:4–7, Paul portrays charity not with abstract adjectives, but with {{c1::15}} active verbs, revealing that Charity is an acting Subject (Christ living in us through the Holy Spirit).
In 1 Corinthians 13:3, the famous textual variant opposes the reading kauthēsomai ('to be burned') with the reading {{c1::kauchēsomai}} ('that I may boast / gain glory').

In 1 Corinthians 13:12, Paul contrasts the blurred reflection of the Corinthian metallic mirror (di' esoptrou en ainigmati) with the Parousia vision of God, which will be {{c1::prosōpon pros prosōpon::[Greek: 'face to face']}}.

Charity is the greatest of the theological triad (1 Cor 13:13) because of Paul's {{c1::eschatological}} perspective: faith yields to vision, hope is fulfilled in possession, but charity endures forever because God is love.

In 1 Corinthians 11:17–22, the scandal at the community agapē was that the wealthy consumed their private meal (idion deipnon) early and became drunk, while the poor were {{c1::humiliated::[h...]}} and remained hungry.

In the Antiochian Eucharistic tradition shared by Paul and Luke, the blessing of the chalice takes place {{c1::after supper::[timing relative to supper]}} (meta to deipnēsai), unlike the consecutive blessing in Mark and Matthew.
According to 1 Corinthians 11:26, every celebration of the Lord's Supper is an active proclamation of the Lord's {{c1::death}} until He comes.
In 1 Corinthians 11:27, receiving the Eucharist unworthily (anaxiōs) makes the recipient {{c1::enochos}} (guilty / liable) of the Body and Blood of the Lord.

In 1 Corinthians 11:29, 'not discerning the body' (mē diakrinōn to sōma) carries two inseparable levels of meaning: the Sacramental Body (Real Presence) and the {{c1::Ecclesial}} Body (the communion of brethren, especially the poor).
In the four-letter Corinthian correspondence, canonical 2 Corinthians represents {{c1::Letter D}}, composed in Macedonia in the autumn of AD 56 after meeting Titus.

The partition hypothesis of Semler and Bultmann views chapters 10–13 of 2 Corinthians as the earlier {{c1::Letter of Tears::[name of letter]}}, whereas the unitary model of Kümmel and De Virgilio defends the unity of the epistle.

In the unitary model of 2 Corinthians, chapters 10–13 shift in tone because Paul directly confronts the obstinate minority influenced by false {{c1::super-apostles::[s...-apostles]}} (hyperlian apostoloi).
The literary genre of 2 Corinthians 6:3–10 is the Hellenistic {{c1::peristasis}} catalogue (list of hardships), which Paul radically transforms into a Christological Theology of the Cross.

Unlike Stoic philosophers who used hardship catalogues to boast of self-sufficiency, Paul boasts in his {{c1::weakness::[w...]}} (astheneia) as the earthen vessel displaying God's transcendent power (2 Cor 4:7; 12:9).
In 2 Corinthians 6:3, Paul states his fundamental ministerial criterion: giving no cause for {{c1::offense::[o...]}} (proskopē) in anything, so that the ministry will not be discredited.
In 2 Corinthians 6:7, Paul describes the apostolic armour as the {{c1::weapons of righteousness}} (hopla tēs dikaiosynēs) for the right hand (sword) and the left (shield).
The climactic seventh paradox of 2 Corinthians 6:10 proclaims the apostle as: {{c1::hōs mēden echontes kai panta katechontes::[Greek: 'as having nothing and yet possessing all things']}}.
